stories.title: Man charged over fatal assault of 18-year-old in Cork
stories.summary: A man in his late teens has been charged as part of an investigation into the fatal assault of an 18-year-old man in Cork city earlier this week. The victim, named locally as Adam McSweeney from Glanmire, was stabbed on Lower Glanmire Road, outside Kent railway station on Tuesday afternoon, after he became involved in an exchange with another group of teenagers. Two males - one in his mid teens and one in his late teens - were arrested and held for questioning. The man in his late teens has since been charged and is due to appear before Cork City District Court this morning. The boy in his mid teens, who was also arrested in relation to the investigation, has been released without charge. Gardaí said a file will be prepared for the National Juvenile Office and the Director of Public Prosecutions.

stories.title: Credit unions informed of October breach yesterday - Troy
stories.summary: Minister of State at the Department of Finance with responsibility for credit unions Robert Troy has written to the Wellington IT - the service provider at the centre of the data breach affecting credit unions - to seek a meeting with them to explain the reason for the delay in informing credit unions of the breach. Yesterday it was reported that a data breach may have compromised details of payees of hundreds of thousands of credit union account holders, such as payee names, account numbers, and addresses. Mr Troy said it is a "major concern" that the company "only made the credit unions aware of this yesterday". The minister said he hopes to "have that meeting very quickly". Wellington IT, based in Northern Ireland, processes member account data on behalf of credit unions. A vulnerability in its systems was exploited by hackers, who managed to gain access to details of payees of hundreds of thousands of credit union account holders, such as payees' names, account numbers and addresses.

stories.title: Anthropic raises record $81 billion in IPO
stories.summary: Anthropic has raised $81.3 billion in the largest stock-market debut on record after upsizing its offering, valuing the Claude chatbot maker at $1.5 trillion in a deal that defies concerns about the AI trade and tech fundraising prospects. The first major frontier AI model developer to go public, Anthropic priced its shares at $83 each, above its initial range of $70 to $78, in a sign of strong demand for the shares from investors. Reuters was first to report earlier yesterday that the company increased the number of shares it was selling by about 19% to 980 million shares. The upsized IPO eclipsed the previous record-setting debut of Elon Musk's SpaceX in June. The total deal size is $107.3 billion, including another $26 billion Anthropic is raising through a private placement of shares at the IPO price, the filings showed. Anthropic comes to the public market as the backdrop for AI stocks has turned challenging. In recent weeks chipmakers and cloud companies, which have raised hundreds of billions of dollars to fund their massive spending plans, have come under pressure due to valuation concerns, mounting AI infrastructure costs and the sudden exit of Nvidia's Jensen Huang, a pillar of the industry's growth.

stories.title: Meet the Ireland Under-17s heading to the World Cup
stories.summary: The Republic of Ireland squad for this year's FIFA Under-17 Men's World Cup in Qatar was finalised last week and has a host of interesting selections. The team is now led by John Cotter, who is part of a new underage coaching system which was announced in May. Before taking the Ireland underage role, Cotter was assistant manager and caretaker manager at Cork City. He was also Colin O'Brien's assistant manager at this tournament last year. O'Brien is no longer with the FAI. Cotter's coaching staff includes Mark Connors, Keith O'Halloran, goalkeeping coach Richard Fitzgibbon and ex-Shelbourne manager and Republic of Ireland defender Joey O'Brien. The squad consists of 21 players from a mix of senior and academy teams from Ireland, England, France, Italy and Austria. Last year nine players came from clubs outside Ireland. This year there are five.
stories.rssSummary: With experience at the back, star power in midfield and talent on the wings and upfront, this year's Republic of Ireland Under-17 squad will look to kick on from the foundations of last year's tournament debut at the World Cup in Qatar.

stories.title: Why the dunnock is so much more than Ireland's 'hedge sparrow'
stories.summary: We present an extract from Birds of Ireland: Symbolism, Myth and Folklore, the new book by Roger O'Reilly. Ireland’s folklore is rich with tales of magical creatures, ancient gods and powerful symbols, but few elements of the natural world hold as prominent a place in Irish myth and legend as our birds. From the soaring eagles of the skies to the humble songbirds that flutter in the hedgerows, Irish birdlife has long been intertwined with stories of transformation, prophecy and spiritual significance. Birds of Ireland is an exploration of how these creatures, both mythical and real, have shaped our understanding of the natural world, the divine, and our place within and sometimes, between both. The dunnock (Prunella modularis), or dunnóg in Irish, is a shy, drab 'little brown job' in the parlance of bird-watchers. Sometimes called the ‘Irish nightingale’ for its loud, rapid song, it’s also known as bráthair an dreoilín (‘friar of the wren’) or máthair-chéile (‘mother-in-law’) in folklore. The welcome sound of the dunnock’s song in the early part of the year has led to an association with Brigid, the goddess of spring and healing. Her feast day falls on 1 February, or the ancient pagan festival of Imbolc – the celebration of the end of winter and the coming of spring. The traditional Gaelic calendar is based on solstices, equinoxes and the change in seasons, and the celebrations of Samhain (Halloween), Bealtaine (the start of summer), Lugnasadh (the start of the autumn harvest), and Imbolc mark the passing of the year. Today, Imbolc or St Brigid’s Day – St Brigid being the Christian version of the goddess – is a national bank holiday and is celebrated by weaving St Brigid’s Crosses from reeds to ward against bad spirits, sickness and ill luck. The dunnock, in common with many birds in ancient folk-lore, was seen as a messenger between worlds and an especially good omen to catch sight of as winter passed and warmth returned to the fields and hedgerows. Ill luck and malevolent spirits, or rather the containment of same, was very much a part of the superstitions that surrounded the dunnock. The dunnock’s blue-green eggs were regarded as charms against evil spirits and were hung on the hearth or along the hob in days gone by. They were especially good for keeping witches and spirits from coming down the chimney! The dunnock's melodies after dark were traditionally believed to reflect lost voices in the spirit world and in more recent times, this belief transitioned in rural Ireland into a conviction that they were the cries of unbaptised babies calling out to their parents from the hereafter. While the dunnock is sometimes referred to as the Irish nightingale, its song has also been described as a rather high-pitched and rapid burst of somewhat tuneless notes, and its hard, raspy 'tcheh’ call has been compared to someone accidentally stepping on a squeaky toy. Because the dunnock is one of the first birds to sing early in spring, it can be forgiven its somewhat squeaky little warble, as by quickly recognising the light of the lengthening days, it reminds us that the dark days of winter will soon be over and the slumbering fields will come alive with the bleat of lambs and the shoots of early flowers. Its piping notes provide a backdrop for the more melodious, visible, but surprisingly less common robin; dunnocks outnumber robins by about three to one. Dunnocks are novel in that both males and females have their own territories. They display unusual breeding behaviour as male birds may have two females, or two males and two females may combine into one breeding pair, depending on how the various territories overlap. Although often referred to as a hedge sparrow, in its favoured environment, the dunnock actually resembles a nervous mouse with its darting, erratic movements close to the ground.

stories.title: Pugh 'disturbed' as she responds to 'stressful' comments
stories.summary: Hollywood actress Florence Pugh has said she is "disturbed" after images of her at the Governors Awards went viral, sparking a flurry of "stressful" online comments about her appearance. The 30-year-old denied speculation that she has undergone cosmetic surgery or used weight-loss injections such as Ozempic, insisting the changes to her appearance are because "I'm looking after myself". The Oppenheimer star shared a lengthy Instagram post on Wednesday addressing the controversy. "I find it so stressful waking up and have thousands of people talking about you and your body in ways that you can’t even comprehend," she wrote. "I woke up the other morning and quite a lot of you were discussing my face and body in such a disturbing way. "I learnt online that I had been on Ozempic? I learnt that I’d had upper bleph? Lower bleph? Filler? Face lipo? Buccal fat remover? Chin surgery? Nose surgery?!"

stories.title: 4 things to do at the 2026 Gifted Craft & Design Fair
stories.summary: Gifted - Ireland's biggest craft, design and artisan food fair - returns to Dublin’s RDS from 2-6 December. With over 30,000 people expected to attend, and 400 exhibitors ready to sell their wares, this event will shine a light on Ireland's independent creative sector. Attendees can meet the makers, enjoy demonstrations and workshops, pick up quality gifts and eat delicious food. Set to host over 100 artisan food producers with gifts and foodie treats to take home, as well as festive treats and flavours for visitors to enjoy at the Christmas Café, the Food Emporium is a must. If you have a sweet tooth, be sure to check out the incredible handmade Irish chocolates from talented makers such as Koko Kinsale, Grá Chocolates, An Olivia Chocolate and Tara Gartlan Chocolate. A resurgence in the Irish ceramics industry has seen Gifted receive a 17% uptick in applications from ceramic artists this year, meaning one in ten exhibitors at the 2026 fair is a ceramicist. This year, attendees will have the opportunity to stop and chat with Irish artists such as Amanda Murphy, Rachel Webb, Marta Ozog and Kathryn Edney.

stories.title: China's Xi to host historic summit with Trump, Putin
stories.summary: The presidents of China, the United States and Russia posed for a photo with other Asia-Pacific leaders ahead of their first trilateral summit, billed by Beijing as talks about "world peace". The three-way meeting between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin at the Kylin Villa in Shenzhen comes with Russia's bloody offensive in Ukraine approaching the five-year mark. Mr Trump is bogged down by his war with Iran that has choked oil supplies and pushed up consumer prices worldwide, and an ascendant China is looking to strengthen its hand in east Asia. The meeting has stoked fears that the three leaders may seek to divide the globe into spheres of influence, for example by deciding the fate of Ukraine over the heads of Kyiv or Europe. Before that, Mr Trump and Mr Xi were due to hold bilateral discussions expected to touch on trade ties and potentially common rules for artificial intelligence, under the cloud of the Nvidia spy scandal. The US leader was also set to meet Mr Putin separately, an official told AFP.

stories.title: Eir's third quarter revemues up 4%, but earnings dip
stories.summary: Telecommunications company eir has reported an increase in third quarter revenues but a fall in earnings, adding that its results were in line with expectations. Eir said its third quarter revenues rose by 4% to €334m, while its EBITDA dipped by 2% to €145m. Its third quarter operating costs fell by 41m to €101m. The company said that nearly 1.6 million premises can connect to fibre to the home (FTTH) broadband across the country, up 7% or 109,000 year on year. A total of 2.3 million premises can now avail of its combined FTTH and FTTC (fibre to the cabinet) networks, or 99% of premises in Ireland. It reported a total of 903,000 fibre broadband connections, up 1% or 13,000, adding that they now total 96% of the company's total broadband base. 61% of customers are on triple or quad-play bundles, up 1% on the same time last year, it added.

stories.title: Marathon champion Jepchirchir banned over doping breach
stories.summary: Kenya's world marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir has been banned for three years for the use of blood booster EPO, the ⁠Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) said, adding that she admitted to breaching anti-doping rules. One of the most decorated women in the sport, the 33-year-old has won gold at the Tokyo Games in 2021 and claimed major marathon victories in New York (2021), Boston (2022), London (2024) and Sydney. The breaches related to the "presence of a prohibited substance or its ‌metabolites or markers in ⁠an athlete's sample" and the "use or attempted use by an athlete of a prohibited substance or a prohibited method", the AIU said. Jepchirchir was given a provisional suspension last month, after testing positive for the banned substance in ‌a sample taken before her Sydney Marathon victory in August. The AIU said the sample returned an ⁠adverse analytical finding (AAF) on 17 September. "In an interview on ‌that same date, the athlete denied using EPO and said ⁠she had ‌no knowledge of how the AAF had occurred," the AIU added.

stories.title: Four Irish authors nominated for 2027 Dublin Literary Award
stories.summary: Four Irish authors and an Irish translator have been nominated for the 2027 Dublin Literary Award, which carries a €100,000 prize for a single work of fiction. The nominations include Mary Costello for A Beautiful Loan, Louise Nealon for Everything That Is Beautiful and Rosamund Taylor for Filly. Irish-British author Maggie O'Farrell is also nominated for Land. Previous award winner and Irish translator Frank Wynne also features on the list for his English translation of French author Jean-Baptiste Andrea’s Watching Over Her. A total of 71 novels have been nominated by 90 libraries across 41 countries. The list includes 30 translated works from 21 languages and 22 debut novels. German writer Nelio Biedermann’s Lázar, translated by Jamie Bulloch, leads the nominations with five. Death and the Gardener by Bulgarian author Georgi Gospodinov, translated by Angela Rodel, has received four nominations. O’Farrell’s Land and The Things We Never Say by American author Elizabeth Strout have each received three nominations.

stories.title: Spanish court opens investigation into Julio Iglesias
stories.summary: A Spanish court has opened an investigation into singer Julio Iglesias after two female ex-employees filed a complaint against him for alleged sexual abuse, which he denies. The announcement marks a turnaround after a first complaint was dismissed on the grounds that Spain had no jurisdiction to try crimes allegedly committed in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic. The women, a domestic worker and a physiotherapist, allege they suffered sexual and other forms of abuse while working at Iglesias's properties in the Caribbean countries in 2021. Iglesias, 83, a Grammy winner with more than 300 million records sold in a decades-long career, has called the allegations "absolutely false". He said he has never "abused, coerced, or disrespected any woman". Madrid's Audiencia Nacional court said in a statement it would investigate alleged "offences against sexual freedom" - which encompass a range of crimes including sexual assault - as well as alleged bodily harm and degrading treatment.

stories.title: Is a 'thermostat war' putting a strain on your relationship?
stories.summary: Architect Roisin Murphy tells Oliver Callan all about the so-called 'thermostat wars' causing bitter rows in people's homes. Listen back above. An American survey published in September revealed that 44% of couples admitted to sneakily changing the temperature dial after their beloved drifted off, while almost two-thirds disagreed about the ideal bedroom temperature and 6% argued about it each night. If this sounds a little close to home, you're not alone. Ahead of speaking to Oliver Callan, Roisin Murphy surveyed her classroom of architecture students about their preferences and was shocked by what she found. "It seems to have been divided by gender", she says. "There are men going to bed with hats and hot water bottles, happily, and socks, and that’s not because they have just refused to turn the heating on. They prefer it cold, and I did not expect that." Murphy adds that it boils down to the kind of house you have, saying, "There’s no domestic disputes if you’re living in a house that’s not retrofitted because it’s usually drafty so women adapt and survive". "But in the retrofitted thermostat world, men take it a bit like the television remote and aren’t giving it back!"

stories.title: Committee recommends independent road safety commissioner
stories.summary: An Oireachtas committee has recommended the establishment of an independent road safety commissioner to co-ordinate road safety activities across departments and agencies. The proposal is one of over 50 made in a report which finds that Ireland has an action plan and a range of bodies working on road safety, yet outcomes have worsened. The report by the Oireachtas Committee on Transport, titled, 'The Urgent Need for Action', is due to be published later. It says that road safety remains a significant public challenge in Ireland, with road deaths increasing, adding that the evidence points to a gap in delivery and accountability. It says a proposed road safety commissioner would be put on a statutory basis, with the authority to monitor delivery and to report publicly where it falls short. It also says that visible enforcement has "thinned" with the garda Roads Policing Unit currently at around 660 members, compared to 1,000 in 2009 and it says that breath-testing "is in decline".

stories.title: UniCredit, Germany reach broad agreement on Commerzbank
stories.summary: UniCredit and Germany have reached agreement on the big sticking points in the Italian bank's takeover of Commerzbank, a major development in the two-year battle for control of the German lender. The agreement, laid out in a letter from UniCredit CEO Andrea Orcel to German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil as well as a separate statement to Reuters from the German minister, states that the merged bank's German headquarters will remain in Frankfurt as a listed entity, a key German demand. But Germany has given up its insistence on naming two supervisory board members to Commerzbank, in a concession to UniCredit. A combination of UniCredit and Commerzbank would create a bank with more than €1.3 trillion in assets across two of the euro zone's largest economies in one of the most significant cross-border European banking deals in years. In the letter dated November 18 and seen by Reuters, Orcel said he was "prepared to commit" to a series of binding principles and thanked Klingbeil for discussions "which have allowed us to find common ground." UniCredit also pledged to put German nationals on UniCredit's board of directors.

stories.title: Boks focusing on rugby as Rassie sets up viewing party
stories.summary: Expect the TV viewing figures to be off the chart on Saturday evening when Ireland and the Springboks finally face off at Aviva Stadium. It remains to be seen, however, how many people are watching the game with their TV on mute. It's no slight on any of the commentary teams calling the play on Saturday evening. Rather, a large chunk of the audience will be listening to Rassie Erasmus's running commentary. Almost exactly 24 hours after being slapped with a six-game ban by World Rugby for comments made at his Monday press conference, the South Africa head coach went to social media and brought some much-needed levity to what has quickly become a toxic week. While Erasmus and the South African rugby union have requested an official hearing from World Rugby regarding his suspension, it appears he has accepted the fact he won't be at Aviva Stadium on Saturday evening. And rather than watch the game on his own, Erasmus wants some company. The former Munster boss is hosting his own online watchalong party, and the website is already up and running.

stories.title: Taoiseach joins leaders in Berlin for meeting on Ukraine
stories.summary: Taoiseach Micheál Martin will join 20 other, mostly European, leaders for a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Berlin today. The ad hoc group of 36 countries has pledged to support Ukraine financially and militarily, including, for some countries, providing security guarantees that might follow a ceasefire. Separately, in Berlin, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will meet European and Ukrainian officials ahead of the next round of talks with Russia, which are unscheduled as yet. Last Friday in Dublin, EU leaders agreed the structure of a negotiating team. This followed a US assurance that Russia had now accepted a European presence at peace negotiations. Yesterday, the European Commission proposed a loan of €45 billion that will go towards Ukraine's budgetary and military needs next year.

That leaves a third quarter-final to be drawn on Thursday. Roscommon won their first Connacht championship since 2019 this year but there is no doubt that all eyes will be on All-Ireland champions Mayo who haven't won the Nestor Cup since 2021. A smarting Galway, who saw their bid for five-in-a-row derailed, will also be out for revenge.

stories.title: New COP 31 draft agreement expected as summit nears end
stories.summary: Negotiators at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya are awaiting the publication of a new draft agreement text that should give the clearest indication yet of what nearly 200 countries are prepared to accept on the future of fossil fuels. The agreement will also state how much help wealthier nations will give poorer ones to cope with a changing climate. The first draft agreement text, published on Monday, ran to 18 pages and included proposals that some countries had already rejected. This next version of what is known as the 'cover decision' should show where those leading the negotiations believe there is room for agreement. There is a lot of interest in whether the 35% electrification figure is included. That is the share of the energy used by households, businesses and transport around the world that the Turkish presidency wants electricity to supply by 2035. Today it is about 23%. The European Union signed up to the voluntary pledge about that on Tuesday.

stories.title: SEAI planning legal action after overclaimed EV grants
stories.summary: The Sustainability Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI) is planning legal action after 15 dealership groups overclaimed demonstration grants for EV vehicles. The Comptroller and Auditor General reported in September that dealerships were overpaid up to €3.9 million in Government grants for electric vehicle demonstration models. The Government has been encouraging the uptake of electric vehicles as part of efforts to reduce transport emissions and meet climate targets. The payments have been administered by the SEAI on behalf of the Department of Transport. However, the Public Accounts Committee will hear this morning that only five dealership groups have paid back the funds to the SEAI in full. SEAI CEO William Walsh will tell TDs that the 15 dealership groups were identified last year through internal checks.

stories.title: Bancroft: Entire team were aware of ball-tampering
stories.summary: Cameron Bancroft on Wednesday claimed that the entire Australian team had known about ball-tampering during a 2018 tour of South Africa, adding that he had lied about the extent of the plot to protect Cricket Australia's investigation into the incident. Bancroft and fellow batsmen David Warner and Steve Smith were banned over the plan to rough up the ball with sandpaper, following an investigation by CA which found that knowledge of the plan was confined to those three players. Australian batter Usman Khawaja's recently released autobiography contradicted the conclusion of the initial CA investigation, however, reigniting the controversy and casting a shadow over Australian cricket. "It was not just the three of us – Steve Smith, David Warner and I — who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team," Bancroft wrote in a lengthy column published in The West Australian. "When I was questioned during Cricket Australia's investigation, I did not give a complete and truthful account. "I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others. I did this to protect Cricket Australia's investigation and not implicate others around me."

stories.title: Call for vigilance after Asian hornet sightings in Dublin
stories.summary: The public is being asked to watch out for Asian hornets after two confirmed sightings of the invasive species in Dublin city. The first report of an Asian hornet was submitted from the Liberties on 8 November, with the second coming three days later on 11 November, from the Grand Canal Dock area of the city. Both sightings were verified by the National Biodiversity Data Centre. The national Asian Hornet Rapid Response Protocol was followed, and the National Parks and Wildlife Service undertook an extensive search and surveillance operation, involving multiple surveys and monitoring measures. However, no evidence of a nest in the Dublin area was found. It is possible the Asian hornets that were sighted were isolated ones. With temperatures dropping across Ireland, any remaining worker hornets are dying off, so active monitoring cannot continue.

stories.title: Van Gogh painting sells for record $190.4m after dispute
stories.summary: A Vincent van Gogh masterpiece sold for a record-breaking $190.4 million (€173.3m) after a dispute between the seller and the heirs of a previous Jewish owner who sold it in the Nazi era, Sotheby's said. 'Chataigniers en fleurs' (Chestnut Trees in Blossom) painted in 1890 in Auvers-sur-Oise, France, set a new record for the Dutch post-Impressionist and became the most expensive work auctioned off so far this season. The previous auction record for a painting by Van Gogh was $117.2m for the 1888 'Orchard with Cypresses' at Christie's in New York in November 2022. An influential German publisher, Samuel Fischer, acquired the painting in Paris in 1909 and his family sold it in 1936. His heirs had previously opposed the sale, saying Fischer's family parted with the painting only because of financial losses suffered under the Nazis. The heirs' Berlin-based lawyer, Gunnar Schnabel, had called on Sotheby's to prove the painting was sold at its market value and that the family would have sold it regardless of the political context.

stories.title: Proposal to lower speed limits in Dublin city
stories.summary: Almost 97% of roads in Dublin city will have speed limits of 30km/h, or a new lower limit of 20km/h, under proposed changes to speed by-laws. The number of roads with speed limits of 50km/h or 60km/h will also drop from almost 10% to just over 3% under the plans, which are to be put out to public consultation. Just over 2.5% of roads in Dublin city will have a new 20km/h limit, with the focus mainly around areas which are partly pedestrianised or that are close to other pedestrian areas. Temple Bar, Henry Street and Talbot Street are among those proposed to be subject to the new lower limits. In a document circulated to members of the Dublin City Council Transport Committee, the council said the proposals were to help improve road safety in the Dublin City Council administrative area. It said that 80 people were killed and more than 2,000 people were seriously injured in road crashes in the Dublin city area in the nine-year period from 2017 to 2025.

stories.title: Ireland's play-off fondue stirs potential summer deja vu
stories.summary: As Troy Parrott and Jack Moylan rippled the nets at Aviva Stadium on Tuesday night, the symbolic value of both goalscorers against Kosovo drew a line back towards seeds planted by Heimir Hallgrimsson in the early days of his Republic of Ireland reign. So watching a striker, who has taken up a perch at Real Betis - by way of AZ Alkmaar - adding the fifth and sixth goals of his UEFA Nations League campaign seemed to fall neatly into place. Hallgrimsson had also long banged the drum for January camps which he could use to take a closer look at emerging players with the potential to establish themselves in the senior picture. While the possibility of using January in such a manner has not yet come to pass, this year the manager and his staff were able to make use of an early summer training camp in Spain followed by three friendlies. It was in that environment that Moylan announced himself to the international stage with aplomb. Granted, the now Cardiff City forward's debut hat-trick might have come in the first of those friendlies - against minnows Grenada. But in the space of six months, the Dubliner has built on that platform to become a key starter and capped a Roy of the Rovers year with a goal and Man of the Match performance yards away from where he held a season ticket not so long ago.

stories.title: Family and football keep Ward focused on biggest rewards
stories.summary: Carla Ward is content and happy with the Republic of Ireland. She has said as much, several times, and previously suggested that if she wanted to return to the WSL she could have done so by now. The 42-year-old places a lot of value in having a happy work-life balance. Ward walked away from Aston Villa in May 2024 because she wanted to spend more time with daughter Hartley. International football is allowing her to show what a talented coach she is without getting swamped by the daily demands of club management. It's expected the FAI will confirm her contract extension sooner rather than later. When asked if she was hopeful it would be boxed off before the first leg of the World Cup play-off final against Poland on 1 December, Ward replied: "Yeah, I’d say so." She also aired a belief that a new deal has never been contingent on the Girls in Green making it to Brazil. That's in contrast to Eileen Gleeson, who paid a heavy price for the narrow loss to Wales in the Euro 2025 play-offs two years ago. "I think we’re just getting started, which sounds crazy, but I feel like we have developed a really clear and clean identity over the last couple of years," said Ward at FAI HQ.

stories.title: Hospital apologises over death that 'shattered' family
stories.summary: The parents of a two-year-old girl who died at Regional Hospital Mullingar in 2023 after being brought in with a fever and high heart rate, have said her death "shattered their lives into a million pieces". Regional Hospital Mullingar this afternoon apologised to the family of Willow Trimble, who the High Court heard died from inflammation of the heart and a very high heart rate, caused by the common viral illness RSV (respiratory syncytial virus). Her lawyers said there was a failure to properly observe and monitor the girl's vital signs after she was brought to hospital on the afternoon of 15 December 2023, and there were "inexplicable delays" in performing an ECG test to monitor heart activity. The court was told that Willow would have survived if she had been transferred to Children's Health Ireland at Crumlin in Dublin in time. In an apology read to the court, Regional Hospital Mullingar Manager Margaret Kelleher said that she offered her sincere and unreserved apology for the failures in care provided to Willow during her time there. She said the hospital deeply regretted the standard of care that she and the family were entitled to expect was not delivered.

stories.title: Govt to spend additional €2.2bn over Budget projections
stories.summary: The Government has agreed to spend €2.2 billion more this year than it had originally planned. Extra spending has been allocated to Social Protection (€625m), Transport (€307m), Foreign Affairs (€252m) and Justice (€103m). This in addition to €780m extra for the for the Department of Health which was agreed at Cabinet yesterday. The additional spending has been allocated for health service delivery, assistance to Ukraine, the Christmas bonus which was announced in last month's Budget, advancing the MetroLink project, targeted energy support measures and additional garda overtime. There are also seven supplementary estimates to reallocate existing funds within departments to cover higher costs using savings or extra tax receipts available elsewhere. In a statement, the Department of Public Expenditure and Reform said: "The Government's approach is to strike the right balance between providing the resources needed to maintain essential public services and responding to emerging pressures, while ensuring that overall expenditure remains sustainable."

stories.title: Prendergast free to play South Africa as citing dismissed
stories.summary: Sam Prendergast will be available for selection for Saturday's Nations Championship clash with South Africa after the citing against him was dismissed. Prendergast was cited by the game's citing commissioner for an alleged hip-drop tackle on Peceli Yato. The incident took place just before the Fijian number 8 scored a try, with him having to leave the field immediately afterwards. But the citing committee of Mike Hamlin and Becky Essex, both from England, and Australia's Wayne Erickson unanimously agreed with the case that Prendergast, Andy Farrell and lawyer Derek Hegarty put forward, agreeing it did not meet the red card threshold. "The Committee unanimously determined that the player had, to the required standard, proved that the citing should be dismissed," read a statement from Nations Championship. The incident became an even bigger talking point after South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus suggested that the Leinster number 10 would get off on a "technicality." Erasmus wasn't able to clarify exactly what he meant during an extraordinary press conference on Monday, with World Rugby subsequently handing him a six-game suspension.
